content: Preventing relapse is a critical aspect of managing quiescent Crohn's disease (CD). While current therapies such as methotrexate, biologics, 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and azathioprine can help maintain remission, they are associated with significant adverse effects. Therefore, there is a need for interventions that are both effective and safe for maintaining remission in CD. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of enteral nutrition for maintaining remission in CD and to assess whether the composition of the nutritional formula impacts its effectiveness. A systematic search of databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, the Cochrane IBD Group Specialized Register, and clinicaltrials.gov, was conducted up to July 27, 2018. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants of any age with quiescent CD were included. Studies comparing enteral nutrition to no intervention, placebo, or other treatments were reviewed. Two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. The primary outcome was clinical or endoscopic relapse, while secondary outcomes included anthropometric measures (e.g., height and weight), quality of life (QoL), adverse events, serious adverse events, and withdrawal due to adverse events. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model, and the GRADE criteria were applied to assess the certainty of evidence. Four RCTs involving 262 adult participants met the inclusion criteria. The studies varied in their comparisons and methodologies, making it impossible to pool the results. The findings are summarized as follows: 1. Elemental Diet vs. Polymeric Diet: The effect of an elemental diet compared to a polymeric diet on remission rates or withdrawal due to adverse events is uncertain. At 12 months, 58% (11/19) of participants in the elemental diet group relapsed compared to 57% (8/14) in the polymeric diet group (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.84; very low certainty evidence). Intolerance to the enteral nutritional formula was higher in the elemental diet group, with 32% (6/19) withdrawing due to taste or smell issues, compared to 0% (0/14) in the polymeric diet group (RR 9.75, 95% CI 0.59 to 159.93; low certainty evidence). Anthropometric measures, QoL, adverse events, and serious adverse events were not reported. 2. Elemental Diet (Half Caloric Needs) vs. Normal Free Diet: The effect of an elemental diet providing half of daily caloric requirements compared to a normal free diet on relapse rates is uncertain. At 12 months, 35% (9/26) of participants in the elemental diet group relapsed compared to 64% (16/25) in the free diet group (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.99; very low certainty evidence). No adverse events were reported. There were no differences in weight change between the two groups. Height and QoL were not reported. 3. Elemental Diet vs. 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP): The effect of an elemental diet compared to 6-MP on relapse rates or adverse events is uncertain. At 12 months, 38% (12/32) of participants in the elemental diet group relapsed compared to 23% (7/30) in the 6-MP group (RR 1.61, 95% CI 0.73 to 3.53; very low certainty evidence). Adverse events occurred in 3% (1/32) of participants in the elemental diet group compared to 13% (4/30) in the 6-MP group (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.98; low certainty evidence). Adverse events in the elemental diet group included surgery due to worsening CD. In the 6-MP group, adverse events included liver injury (n=2), hair loss (n=1), and surgery due to an abscess (n=1). No serious adverse events or withdrawals due to adverse events were reported. Weight, height, and QoL were not reported. 4. Polymeric Diet vs. Mesalamine: The effect of a polymeric diet compared to mesalamine on relapse rates and weight is uncertain. At 6 months, 42% (18/43) of participants in the polymeric diet group relapsed compared to 55% (22/40) in the mesalamine group (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.19; low certainty evidence). The mean difference in weight gain was 1.9 kg higher in the polymeric diet group compared to the mesalamine group (95% CI -4.62 to 8.42; low certainty evidence). Adverse events in the polymeric diet group included nausea (n=2) and diarrhea (n=4). It is unclear if any adverse events occurred in the mesalamine group. Height, QoL, serious adverse events, and withdrawal due to adverse events were not reported. The authors concluded that the evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of enteral nutrition for maintaining remission in quiescent CD is highly uncertain. No definitive conclusions can be drawn at this time. Further research is needed to clarify the role of enteral nutrition as a maintenance therapy in CD. Four ongoing studies with an estimated enrollment of 280 participants may provide additional insights, and this review will be updated when their results become available.
